summary: This standards-track RFC describes procedures to damp Multicast VPN routing state changes, controlling the churn caused by multicast dynamics in customer sites. Inspired by BGP unicast route damping, they help avoid uncontrolled control-plane load in the core.

plainLanguage.summary: If a switch keeps flickering, you ignore some flickers so the network is not constantly updating.

questions: what is multicast vpn state damping
what are the default mvpn damping values
subtitle: Keeps multicast VPN routers from flooding the core with join and prune churn by delaying prunes for flapping state.

tldr.problem: Receivers in customer sites join and leave multicast groups far more often than unicast routes change, and that churn can overload the BGP and tunnel control planes of a shared provider network.
tldr.mechanism: A router tracks a decaying figure-of-merit for each multicast state, borrowed from BGP route flap damping. When it passes a cutoff, the router holds the state active and delays prune propagation upstream until the figure decays below a reuse threshold.
tldr.outcome: The control-plane load has an upper bound that the operator tunes, at the cost of a modest increase in bandwidth on upstream links. The RFC updates RFC 6514.

today: RFC 7899 is a Proposed Standard from June 2016 and updates RFC 6514. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multicast State Needs Damping
sections.content:
In a BGP-based multicast VPN (RFC 6513, RFC 6514), receivers joining and leaving groups through IGMP and MLD make routers adjust multicast routing state and provider tunnel state. Multicast membership follows application behavior, so it can legitimately change much more often than typical unicast routing.

In a VPN, isolation between customers of a shared infrastructure is a core requirement, so the expectations about denial-of-service risk are strict. The load on the BGP control plane and the provider tunnel (P-tunnel) setup control plane therefore needs to stay under control whatever the end hosts do.

Section 16 of RFC 6514 already called for damping C-multicast and Leaf Auto-discovery routes by delaying withdrawals. This RFC supplies the detail and the operator controls, which is why it updates RFC 6514.
sections.plainLanguage: If everybody in a huge group kept changing their mind every second, the postman would never stop carrying updates. This RFC gives the network a way to calm that down.

sections.title: The Basic Idea: Delay the Prune
sections.content:
Operators configure multicast VPN Provider Edge routers (PEs) so that, when the rate of change of a multicast state passes a configurable threshold, they delay propagating prune messages to other PEs. Joins are not affected. For the downstream router, such as the Customer Edge router, nothing changes, and bandwidth on the PE-CE link does not grow.

The cost lands upstream: a flow is forwarded for longer than it would be without damping, so average bandwidth on a PE-PE link rises. The RFC says damping events more frequent than one per X seconds can be handled without adding more than X seconds to the time a flow stays on a link, and that simulation of the exponential decay algorithm shows churn dropping drastically without a significant bandwidth increase. The exception is a network with strict multicast bandwidth limits, where the extra forwarding time could cause congestion.

The RFC avoids the unicast word "suppressed" and says damping is "active" or "inactive", because the multicast state is held active rather than hidden.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining a game happens right away. Leaving is announced a bit late if you keep going in and out. Your own game is never affected, but the scoreboard keeper has less to write down.

sections.title: Why Existing Mechanisms Fall Short
sections.content:
The RFC reviews three alternatives and finds each unsuitable.

  • Rate-limiting PIM messages (Section 5.3.3 of RFC 4609) impacts the service delivered and has side effects on legitimate users.
  • PIM prune override and IGMP/MLD timers can give a de facto form of damping, but they need extra bandwidth on the PE-CE link, require disabling explicit tracking, can clash with fast-leave behavior on some implementations, offer little configurability, and cannot tell flows apart by how dynamic they are.
  • BGP route flap damping (RFC 2439, RFC 7196) is not specified for multicast, and it suppresses a damped route, while the goal here is to keep advertising it.

Still, the standardized exponential decay parameters of BGP damping can be reused, which gives operators familiar, consistent configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Other fixes were tried on paper: slowing every message, or using old waiting timers. They either hurt normal users or were too blunt, so a new approach was written.

sections.title: The Damping Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure reuses ideas from RFC 2439 and applies to (S,G) states in PIM-SM, including those created through IGMP or MLD, and to (*,G) states for Any-Source Multicast groups. It does not damp (S,G,Rpt) Prune state. The key terms are:

  • figure-of-merit: a number estimating recent activity of a state. It starts at zero and decays exponentially between events.
  • decay-half-life: the time for the figure-of-merit to halve with no events. Implementations REQUIRED to let operators set it in seconds.
  • cutoff-threshold: damping is applied above this value.
  • reuse-threshold: damping stops below this value.
  • increment-factor: how much each state update event adds.

When a change arrives on a downstream interface that changes the PIM downstream state machine, the router MUST apply normal PIM processing for downstream traffic, update the figure-of-merit, add the increment, and activate damping if the figure is strictly above the cutoff. While damping is active, the upstream state machine is held in Joined state: Joins may be sent as refreshes, but no Prune is sent. When the figure falls strictly below the reuse threshold, the upstream state is recomputed and a Join or Prune goes upstream as appropriate.

An implementation MUST keep explicit (S,G) state while damping is active. Prunes caused by keep-alive timer expiry, PIM Assert changes, RPF neighbor updates, and switching between the Rendezvous Point Tree and Shortest Path Tree are not delayed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flicker adds a point to a score that slowly drains away. If the score gets too high, the router waits to say goodbye until the score drains low enough.

sections.title: MVPN and P-Tunnel Procedures
sections.content:
In a multicast VPN, the PIM procedures can run in the VRF PIM instance (the "C-PIM instance"), where not sending a Prune means not withdrawing the C-multicast Source Tree Join BGP route. An implementation of RFC 6513 that uses PIM to carry C-multicast routing MUST support this to comply.

Where BGP carries C-multicast routing (RFC 6514), damping can instead be applied inside BGP to Source Tree Join, Shared Tree Join and Leaf A-D routes. The changes are: do not withdraw damped routes (rather than not advertising them), allow the half-life in seconds, and use multicast-specific parameters. Route Reflectors and ASBRs can also apply it, and an implementer MUST implement at least one of the PIM or BGP approaches, with the BGP one recommended for RRs and ASBRs.

Withdrawals caused by a change of Upstream Multicast Hop or Upstream Multicast PE SHOULD NOT be damped when not all routers can drop traffic from the wrong PE. In that case an implementation MUST either not damp them by default or offer a knob to disable it, and damping on RRs and ASBRs is RECOMMENDED against, since they cannot tell what caused a withdrawal.

For selective P-tunnels, a PE MUST damp Leaf A-D routes like C-multicast routes, and MUST damp activity related to removing itself from a P-tunnel. How depends on the tunnel type: PIM-based tunnels reuse the PIM damping, mLDP tunnels get a similar technique, and root-initiated tunnels (P2MP RSVP-TE or ingress replication) need nothing extra if Leaf A-D damping is in place. Implementations of RFC 7117 (Ethernet VPN multicast) MUST follow the same P-tunnel procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The same waiting trick is used wherever the customers' groups are carried across the provider's network, including the shared delivery paths the provider builds.

sections.title: Operations and Default Values
sections.content:
The procedures would be enabled on PE routers, and with BGP-based C-multicast routing also on ASBRs and RRs. Tools to observe and troubleshoot damping are needed, and showing damping information next to multicast state is RECOMMENDED for C-multicast routing states and P-tunnel states.

Because streams are always delivered unchanged and only bandwidth is traded, the defaults are conservative. The RFC RECOMMENDS: increment-factor 1000, cutoff-threshold 3000, decay-half-life 10s and reuse-threshold 1500. The default maximum figure-of-merit is 20 times the increment factor, 20000. Proposed maximums are a half-life of 60 s and a cutoff of 50000.

With those defaults, a state updated less often than once every 6 s is never damped, and one changing once per second for 3 s is not damped either. One changing once per second for 4 s is damped after the fourth change for approximately 13 s. At the maximum figure, traffic may flow for approximately 37 s after activity stops.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggested settings are mild, so normal use is never slowed, and only very restless groups get the waiting treatment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the procedures add no new security issues and aim to reduce denial-of-service risk without the downside of mechanisms like rate-limiting. The protection covers the control plane of multicast routing protocols, but only for the updates a router sends upstream. It does not reduce the load of processing information from downstream neighbors. That needs damping on those neighbors or peers, or at the network edge. Protection against customer-facing or other-domain interfaces is out of scope and should use mechanisms such as RFC 4609.

To be effective, damping must be paired with configuration that limits how many multicast states can be created. The two may interact, since a state with a pending prune can still count for a while. Finally, damping addresses averaged load, not peaks.
sections.plainLanguage: This helps the router tell fewer updates upstream, but it does not stop a flood coming in. Other limits are still needed for that.

items.title: figure-of-merit
items.text: Activity score for one state; decays exponentially.

items.title: increment-factor
items.text: Added to the score on each state update.

items.title: decay-half-life
items.text: Time for the score to halve with no events.
